t: Long described as invaders from South America who conquered the earlier Igneri, the Kalinago appear from archaeology and ancient DNA to have formed from the islands’ own peoples together with newcomers from the mainland.

They kept their independence in the Lesser Antilles against Spain and later France and England; Dominica and Saint Vincent were left to them as reserves in 1660, but the British had annexed both by 1763.

On Saint Kitts in 1626 English and French settlers massacred an estimated 2,000 Kalinago, and Spanish tales of Carib cannibalism, never backed by hard evidence, have been read as a campaign to justify such genocidal expeditions.
dyk: The English word “cannibal” comes from the Kalinago word karibna, “person”, after Columbus spread stories of man-eating Caribs that he had apparently heard from their Taíno enemies.
ev: By the traditional account, Caribs migrate from the Orinoco region of South America to the islands
Columbus reaches the Caribbean and hears from the Taíno of Carib raids
English and French settlers massacre an estimated 2,000 Kalinago at Bloody Point on Saint Kitts
France and England make the Treaty of Saint Charles with the Kalinago, leaving them Dominica and Saint Vincent as reserves
Britain has annexed Saint Lucia, Tobago, Dominica and Saint Vincent
After the Second Carib War the British expel the Garifuna of Saint Vincent to Honduras
The British government grants the Kalinago a territory of 3,700 acres on the east coast of Dominica
Dominica officially changes the people’s name from Carib to Kalinago

f.homeland: The Lesser Antilles: at Spanish contact the Windward Islands, Dominica and the southern Leeward Islands, including Guadeloupe, and possibly Barbados; Grenada and Saint Vincent; today the Kalinago Territory, 3,700 acres on the east coast of Dominica; a Carib community at Arima in Trinidad; the related Garifuna in Central America.
f.period: Cayo pottery in the islands c. 1000–1500, reaching Grenada and Saint Vincent around 1250; the change from Igneri to Island Carib culture perhaps around 1450; Spanish contact from 1492; the massacre on Saint Kitts, 1626; the Treaty of Saint Charles, 1660; British annexation of Dominica and Saint Vincent by 1763; the Garifuna expelled in 1797; the Carib Territory granted in 1903; the name Kalinago official in Dominica in 2015.
f.known: dugout canoes and voyages between the islands; fishing; raids, and resistance to Spanish, French and English colonisers; the “poison arrow curtain”; an Arawakan language with a men’s Cariban pidgin; ancestors’ bones kept in the house; Cayo and Suazan Troumassoid pottery; bush medicine
f.sources: the accounts of Columbus and the Spanish; missionaries such as Raymond Breton (in the islands 1635–1653), Cesar de Rochefort and Jean Baptiste Labat; archaeology of Cayo and Suazan Troumassoid pottery in Grenada and Saint Vincent, with radiocarbon dating; ancient DNA; the work of Irving Rouse, William F. Keegan and Corinne L. Hofman; Kalinago oral testimony and communities today.
